subject: Architecture
title: Çatalhöyük: A City Without Streets
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Çatalhöyük: A City Without Streets.

hook.text: Nine thousand years ago, 8,000 people lived in a Turkish settlement with no streets or doors.

buildup.text: Houses were packed wall to wall. Residents entered through holes in the roof using ladders.

discovery.text: The design made defense easy — attackers faced a solid wall of rooftops with no way in.

twist.text: Families buried their dead under the floor and continued living above them for generations.

climax.text: Çatalhöyük thrived for 2,000 years — one of the longest-occupied settlements in history.

punchline.text: No streets, no doors, no government. Just rooftops and community.

quiz.question: How did residents of Çatalhöyük enter their homes?
options: Through front doors at street level
Through holes in the roof using ladders

details.summary: Çatalhöyük in Turkey, inhabited from roughly 7500 to 5700 BCE, was a densely packed settlement of up to 8,000 people with no streets — residents entered their mud-brick homes through holes in the roof using ladders. The rooftops themselves served as the city's public space and circulation network.
details.whyItMatters: Çatalhöyük challenges every modern assumption about city planning. A city without streets, where roofs are roads and entry is from above, proves that humans can organize urban life in ways radically different from anything we consider normal.
takeaways: Up to 8,000 people lived in a settlement with no streets
Residents entered homes through rooftop openings via ladders
Rooftops served as the public circulation and gathering space

faq.question: Why were there no streets at Çatalhöyük?
faq.answer: Buildings were packed together sharing walls for structural support and thermal mass. The honeycomb layout may have served defense — with no ground-level doors, intruders couldn't easily enter. Rooftop circulation also kept living spaces cleaner by separating foot traffic from interiors.

faq.question: What did houses look like inside?
faq.answer: Interiors were surprisingly decorated — walls were plastered and sometimes painted with hunting scenes and geometric designs. Built-in platforms served as seating and sleeping areas. Some houses contained burials beneath the floor. Ovens and storage bins were built into the structure.
